title: The Boot Sequence: How to Start from Any Database
body:
Every database in the network opens the same way: read its tagline, open one full record, run its demo, then follow one link outward. That four-step boot works whether you start at equations, words, wiki, or all-worlds-data, because every database carries the same anatomy: a full record, a demo program, a working version, and links to its neighbours.

Starting from any database is not a detour. The network is built so that the first database you touch teaches you the shape of all the rest, and the second database you touch teaches you what makes it different. Boot from the database closest to your question, not from a hub page, and let the records pull you sideways.
demo_output:
1. Read the tagline
2. Open one full record
3. Run its demo
4. Follow one link outward
Boot complete: you now know the shape of every database.

title: Special Use: The Math and Equation Family
body:
The equation family, anchored by equations, is uniquely good for checking your own work. Its records are solved problems with answers you can verify by substitution in seconds, which makes it the network's pocket calculator and its honesty school at once: a claim that can be checked is checked, on the spot.

Special use: when any other database makes a numerical claim, boot the equation family, restate the claim as an equation, and solve it. If the arithmetic holds, the claim survives its first test; if it does not, you have found the exact step where it breaks.

title: Special Use: Patents, Specs, and the Making Family
body:
The making family — patents for harvested public records and specs for original drafts — is uniquely good for turning an idea into a buildable thing. A patent record shows what has already been claimed; a spec draft shows a complete filing-shaped design with manufacture notes, a runnable program, and a demo.

Special use: start at a patent when you want prior art, start at a spec when you want a design you can extend, and move between them whenever a new idea needs both a lineage and a workshop. No other family carries a design from idea to runnable code in a single record.

print('patents: what has already been claimed (public record)')
print('specs:   a complete design, manufacture notes, runnable demo')
print('Move patent -> spec whenever an idea needs a lineage AND a workshop.')

title: Special Use: Words, Wiki, and the Knowledge Family
body:
The knowledge family — words for definitions and wiki for encyclopedia articles — is uniquely good for settling what a word means before you argue about it. Every downstream database leans on definitions, so a dispute that starts in a technical database is often resolved fastest by booting the dictionary.

Special use: when two databases seem to contradict each other, check whether they are using the same word differently. Nine times out of ten the contradiction is a definition gap, and the dictionary record closes it without touching either database.

title: Special Use: Books, Comics, Music, and the Story Family
body:
The story family — books, comics, music, and games — is uniquely good for complete works. These databases do not describe stories; they carry them, whole, with chapters, art, songs, and playable rules, which makes them the network's proof that a database can hold a finished thing, not just facts about it.

Special use: boot the story family when you want to see what finished looks like. A complete book is the standard every other database's full record is measured against: whole, readable, and usable as-is.

title: Special Use: Tools, Computers, Chips, and Apps
body:
The tool family — computers, chips, apps, and fixit — is uniquely good for doing. Where the knowledge family explains and the story family shows, the tool family hands you a working version: a program to run, a chip to study, a repair to follow step by step.

Special use: whenever a record in any other family ends with "how does it work?", boot the tool family and run the demo. A working version answers the question in a way prose cannot, and a failed demo tells you exactly what is still missing.

title: Special Use: Earth, Flight, Transport, and the World Family
body:
The world family — earth, flight, transportation, and photography — is uniquely good for grounding abstractions in places, routes, and views. A design that works on paper meets weather, distance, and terrain here, and a photograph records what a place actually looked like at a stated time.

Special use: boot the world family before you declare a plan finished. If a route cannot be flown, a vehicle cannot be driven there, or a photograph contradicts the description, the plan is not finished yet.

title: Special Use: The Umbrella Databases
body:
The umbrella databases — all-worlds-data and all-universal-data — are uniquely good for orientation. They do not replace the databases they point at; they inventory them, so a new user can see the shape of the whole network before diving into any single part.

Special use: boot an umbrella when you are lost, not when you have a question. A question goes to the database that answers it; being lost goes to the umbrella, which shows you where the answering databases live.

title: Starter Workflow: Franchise to Crossover to Game to Fun
body:
Workflow one combines four families in order. Start at a franchise pair in books or comics and read one complete work. Move to crossover records to see how two worlds blend. Turn the blend into a game concept in games, with rules you can actually play. Finish in the fun generators, where the concept becomes something you can run tonight.

Each step hands the next step a finished thing, never a sketch: a book, a crossover, a rule set, a playable generator. If any step cannot hand over a finished thing, stop there and finish it; the workflow only works because nothing downstream is asked to build on a stub.
demo_output:
1. books/comics: read one complete work
2. crossovers: blend two worlds
3. games: write playable rules
4. fun generators: run it tonight
Rule: each step hands the next a FINISHED thing.

title: Starter Workflow: Patent to Spec to Product
body:
Workflow two turns prior art into a product. Start at patents and find the closest public record to your idea. Move to specs and draft your own version, with manufacture notes and a runnable program. Carry the draft into computers or chips for a working version, and into mall when the thing is ready to be shown as a product.

The workflow's honesty rule is its spine: the patent step is labeled public record, the spec step is labeled original draft, and the two are never blurred. A product built this way can show its whole lineage, from prior art to finished design, in four hops.

chain=['patents: find the closest public record','specs: draft your own version','computers/chips: build a working version','mall: show it as a product']
for i,s in enumerate(chain,1): print(f'{i}. {s}')
demo_output:

title: Starter Workflow: Word to Wiki to Book to Check
body:
Workflow three turns curiosity into verified understanding. Start at words and pin the definition. Move to wiki for the full article and its context. Read a complete treatment in books if one exists. Then check the result: run the validity suite on any numerical or factual claim the journey produced, and cite the public sources with the citations database.

This workflow is the network's study method in miniature. Definition first, context second, depth third, verification last — and the verification step is not optional, because a journey that ends in an unchecked claim has only moved the unknown, not removed it.

title: First-Run Guide for a New User
body:
First run, in full. One: pick the database closest to your question and boot it with the four-step sequence. Two: open one full record and read it to the end. Three: run its demo, and if the demo fails, note exactly what failed — that note is useful. Four: follow one link outward and repeat. Five: when you have an answer, verify it and cite it before you pass it on.

You do not need to learn the whole network first. The network is designed so that any single database teaches the pattern, any workflow teaches the combinations, and the suites — boot, mix-review, validity, citations, verification — teach the discipline of using it well. Start anywhere; the structure carries you.

print('First run:')

print('Start anywhere; the structure carries you.')
